sweep_summary: Both works with stress in the title are duplicate Glottolog records of one work, Hildebrandt 2005 (LTBA 28.1), which is already held (image-only scan + scanned) and was re-read: its suprasegmental section is entirely about word tone and it is silent on stress placement except one incidental 'unstressed (second) syllable' remark on p. 15, consistent with the catalog's root-initial coding. The catalog's deciding passage (Hildebrandt 2004, §2.6, pp. 37-39) was re-verified verbatim in the text we hold layer and stays the best first-hand statement; nothing read supersedes it. One new, weaker datum: the AUTOTYP Word Domains database (Bickel, Hildebrandt & Schiering; refetched from GitHub) codes Manange as 'Exactly 1 Main Stress, Penult' over 'stem ± prefix ± suffix ± particle' from 'Grammar Explicit' evidence, a label that diverges from 'root-initial' whenever a root is polysyllabic or prefixed; this is a secondary coding and merits a note, not a reclassification. Unread candidates worth acquiring: Hildebrandt & Anderson 2023 'Word Prominence in Languages of Southern Asia' (OUP, high), Hildebrandt 2015 'The Prosodic Word' (OUP handbook, medium), Bickel, Hildebrandt & Schiering 2009 (De Gruyter, medium; source of the AUTOTYP coding), Hildebrandt 2013/2018 CUP sketch (low). sealang.net unreachable; DOI landing for the LTBA paper (dr.ntu.edu.sg) behind an AWS WAF captcha; OUP/Cambridge pages show no abstract.

tone_statements.quote: Tone in Manange is diachronically more phonologized than in other Bodish languages in that contrastive pitch is now the primary correlate to tone, and other correlates are secondary in that they do not apply for all of the tones (cf. Mazaudon 1977). ... Manange has four tones aligning primarily along a parameter of contrastive vowel pitch. ... there are two low tones and two high tones, with a further division into level and falling tones. ... As with other Bodish languages, the TBU in Manange is the P-word, including the mono- or polysyllabic root or stem morpheme and bound affixes and clitics. ... phonologically bound grammatical morphemes are inherently toneless.

tone_statements.citation: Mazaudon, Martine. 1978. Consonantal mutation and tonal split in the Tamang sub-family of Tibeto-Burman. Kailash: A Journal of Himalayan Studies 6(3): 157-179.
tone_statements.quote: Each monosyllabic word, in languages of the TGTM group, can carry one of four tones. ... [§3.12 table, column MANANGBA Ngawal:] tone-1 33 tone-2 45 tone-3 54 tone-4 31 ... [§3.21] In Manangba the system is even more different. There is no use of breathy vs. clear voice quality, but rather a normal voice for the two lower tones and a very tense quality for the two high tones. The two higher tones here are not /1/ and /2/ as expected, but /3/ and /2/. Tone-1 is lower-mid level, and tone-4 is a fall from mid to low.
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Four word-tones (all TGTM); Ngawal Manangba 33, 45, 54, 31. Manangba: no breathy/clear split, tense voice on the two high tones (/3/, /2/); tone-1 lower-mid level, tone-4 mid-to-low fall. Suffixes toneless, root tone spreads over the word. Intro calls TGTM 'marginally tonal'. Nothing on stress.

Some words, especially recent loanwords, do not carry a tone melody. While most stems and roots are monosyllabic, there are also some disyllabic noun roots and some compound verb stems.

tone_statements.quote: Manange has four tones aligning primarily along a parameter of contrastive vowel pitch. [...] As with the other Bodish languages, there are two low tones and two high tones, with a further division into level and falling tones. [...] Only words with unaspirated obstruent onsets occur in tone /3/, while only words with aspirated onsets occur in tone /4/. This split is not observed for words with sonorant initials, such that F0 is the primary tonal correlate. || As with other Bodish languages, the TBU in Manange is the P-word, including the mono- or polysyllabic root or stem morpheme and bound affixes and clitics. So, a single pitch trajectory also spreads across morphologically complex P-words. [...] The F0 values spread from root across suffix syllables, indicating that phonologically bound grammatical morphemes are inherently toneless. || The findings indicate that Urban speakers show a large-scale phonetic merger of the four tones into a two-way (high-low) opposition.

sources.quote: Manange has four tones aligning primarily along a parameter of contrastive vowel pitch. [...] As with the other Bodish languages, there are two low tones and two high tones, with a further division into level and falling tones. [...] Only words with unaspirated obstruent onsets occur in tone /3/, while only words with aspirated onsets occur in tone /4/. This split is not observed for words with sonorant initials, such that F0 is the primary tonal correlate. || As with other Bodish languages, the TBU in Manange is the P-word, including the mono- or polysyllabic root or stem morpheme and bound affixes and clitics. So, a single pitch trajectory also spreads across morphologically complex P-words. [...] The F0 values spread from root across suffix syllables, indicating that phonologically bound grammatical morphemes are inherently toneless. || The findings indicate that Urban speakers show a large-scale phonetic merger of the four tones into a two-way (high-low) opposition.

sources.quote: Each monosyllabic word, in languages of the TGTM group, can carry one of four tones. ... [§3.12 table, column MANANGBA Ngawal:] tone-1 33 tone-2 45 tone-3 54 tone-4 31 ... [§3.21] In Manangba the system is even more different. There is no use of breathy vs. clear voice quality, but rather a normal voice for the two lower tones and a very tense quality for the two high tones. The two higher tones here are not /1/ and /2/ as expected, but /3/ and /2/. Tone-1 is lower-mid level, and tone-4 is a fall from mid to low.
sources.note: Four word-tones (all TGTM); Ngawal Manangba 33, 45, 54, 31. Manangba: no breathy/clear split, tense voice on the two high tones (/3/, /2/); tone-1 lower-mid level, tone-4 mid-to-low fall. Suffixes toneless, root tone spreads over the word. Intro calls TGTM 'marginally tonal'. Nothing on stress.
